newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: SIMEX Taiwan futures seen gaining from lift of b.
newsitem.headline: SIMEX Taiwan futures seen gaining from lift of b.

text.p: Singapore's futures exchange is likely to be the main beneficiary of a potential move by Taiwanese authorities to allow local trading of offshore stock index futures, traders and analysts said on Wednesday.
Taiwan's Finance Minister Paul Chiu told parliament on Wednesday that his ministry was "leaning towards" lifting the ban and that a decision would be made by the end of April.

Taiwan stock index futures and options, launched separately by the Singapore International Monetary Exchange (SIMEX) and Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME) on January 9, have made slow progress, due largely to the absence of Taiwanese retail interest, dealers said.

Although turnover on SIMEX has overtaken the CME, with daily volumes exceeding 700 lots on average, dealers continue to complain about a lack of liquidity and strong customer interest. But with signs of an impending suspension of the ban and the passage of Taiwan's own long-delayed Futures Trading Law, traders said they expected SIMEX to attract much of the resulting growth in business.

"I think we'd see volumes at least double. Retail investors would provide added volume to what we already see, which consists mainly of institutional use of the Taiwanese derivatives market," said Perry Gilbert, vice president of Refco (Singapore) Pte Ltd.

Despite not being able to trade the offshore contracts officially, Gilbert said Taiwane investors had shown an interest in the SIMEX MSCI Taiwan index contract and kept abreast of its performance through brokers here.
"Taiwanese retail punters who control 95 percent of the volume will clearly go to SIMEX," said Richard Fan, associate director of equity derivatives at W.I. Carr in Hong Kong.
Fan said SIMEX's pit-based trading system would draw wider interest than the electronic after-hours GLOBEX system used by the CME.

He said the futures had been trading consistently at a discount to the cash market because foreign institutions, the most active players so far, were using them as a hedge by going short and buying the cash stocks.
"Now it'll make clear economic sense for retail investors to get in and buy these futures and short the stocks against them," Fan said.
